c.tagline: Sherry, flamenco and dancing horses under the Andalusian sun.

taxi.fareNote: Andalusian taxis are white with a green light when free; fares are metered with fixed supplements for the airport and luggage. Uber is limited, but Cabify and Free Now operate in the area.

emergency.note: 112 is the single EU-wide emergency number connecting to police, fire and ambulance.

avoid.reason: Pickpocketing rises sharply in festival crowds during the Feria and Semana Santa; keep valuables secure.

hood_desc: The walkable historic heart around Plaza del Arenal, the Alcázar, the cathedral and the great sherry bodegas of González Byass and Fundador; where first-timers stay to have the sights, tabancos and shopping at their door.

The old gypsy quarter widely called the cradle of flamenco, a maze of whitewashed lanes around the Church of Santiago that comes alive with peñas and the Festival de Jerez; steeped in atmosphere and song.
A historic parish district around the ornate Gothic-Isabelline Church of San Miguel, close to the train station and the Tabanco tapas scene; central, traditional and handy for arrivals.

Also known as San Pedro, an old quarter just outside the line of the walls east of the centre, built around the church of San Pedro and Plaza de San Andrés; bodegas, tabancos and ordinary local streets rather than tourist sights.
A quieter, elegant old-town parish around Plaza de San Mateo and the Museo Arqueológico, with churches, palaces and a relaxed local feel a few minutes' walk from the center.

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink throughout the city.

transit.hours: Urban buses run roughly 6:30 AM to 11:00 PM; the Cercanías C-1 line links Jerez, its airport, El Puerto and Cádiz through the day.
transit.note: Jerez has no metro or tram; the flat, compact old town is easily walked, with city buses and Renfe Cercanías / Media Distancia trains handling the airport and trips to Cádiz, El Puerto de Santa María and Seville.
transit.pay: Pay cash or with the Tarjeta Bus travel card on city buses; buy Renfe tickets from station machines or counters. All fares are in euros.

bus: Intercity coaches (Comes, Damas) to Cádiz, Seville and the Costa de la Luz
train: Jerez railway station (Renfe Cercanías C-1, Media Distancia and long-distance to Seville, Cádiz and Madrid)

transit.m: Renfe Cercanías C-1 train from Aeropuerto station to Jerez center (~10 min)
Bus line M-050 to the city center (~25 min)
Taxi to the city center (~12-15 min)

tip.r: Not expected; locals round up or leave small change, and about 5-10% for good restaurant service is generous.

food.name: Berza jerezana
food.desc: Winter stew of chickpeas, white beans and greens enriched with pringa, the shredded pork, chorizo and morcilla cooked down into it.

places.name: Bar Juanito
places.note: Jerez tapas institution since 1943; the berza is a fixture of its traditional menu.

places.name: Tabanco Plateros
places.note: Classic tabanco pairing small bowls of traditional stew with sherry from the barrel.

places.name: La Cruz Blanca
places.note: Always-busy old-town bar known for guisos and generous tapas portions.

food.name: Ajo caliente
food.desc: Thick garlic, tomato and bread mash worked with olive oil until creamy; the dish vineyard workers lived on out in the albariza vineyards.

places.name: Tabanco El Pasaje
places.note: The oldest tabanco in Jerez, with live flamenco and rustic tapas at the barrel.

places.name: Bar Juanito
places.note: Keeps the old country recipes on the menu year-round, not just in season.

places.name: Tabanco Las Banderillas
places.note: Traditional bar known for marinated potatoes, ham and other old Jerez tapas.

food.name: Rinones al Jerez
food.desc: Lamb or veal kidneys flash-fried with garlic and finished with a splash of oloroso until the sauce turns dark and glossy; mopped up with bread.

places.name: Bar Juanito
places.note: One of the tapas the bar built its reputation on, cooked with local sherry.

places.name: La Cruz Blanca
places.note: Standing-room bar where sherry-cooked offal tapas come fast and cheap.

places.name: Tabanco Plateros
places.note: Small kitchen turning out sherry-sauced classics to go with a copa of fino.

food.name: Alcachofas a la montillana
food.desc: Artichoke hearts slow-braised in olive oil, garlic and dry sherry with a little ham; a spring speciality Jerez bars are famous for.

places.name: Bar Juanito
places.note: Its artichokes are the single most-ordered tapa and the reason many people come.

places.name: Albores
places.note: Modern Andalusian kitchen in the centre giving classic vegetable tapas a lighter treatment.

places.name: La Carbona
places.note: Restaurant inside an old bodega, cooking traditional dishes designed around sherry pairings.

food.name: Rabo de toro
food.desc: Oxtail braised for hours with vegetables and a heavy pour of oloroso until the meat slides off the bone; served with fried potatoes.

places.name: La Carbona
places.note: Old bodega dining room; long-braised meats matched glass by glass with sherry.

places.name: Albores
places.note: Central restaurant well regarded for its stews and updated Andalusian classics.

places.name: La Cruz Blanca
places.note: Serves the oxtail as both a tapa and a full plate, a good way to try it cheaply.

food.name: Tocino de cielo
food.desc: Dense egg-yolk custard under burnt caramel, invented when Jerez convents were given the yolks left over from bodegas clarifying their wine.

places.name: Convento de Santa Maria de Gracia
places.note: Nuns still sell convent sweets through a turntable window; the original source of the recipe.

places.name: Bar Juanito
places.note: Traditional dessert list keeps tocino de cielo alongside sherry-soaked classics.

places.name: Albores
places.note: Reliable version of the city's signature dessert in a comfortable sit-down setting.

food.name: Sherry
food.desc: Fino and manzanilla bone-dry and chilled, then amontillado, oloroso and syrupy Pedro Ximenez; poured by the glass straight from the barrel.

places.name: Tabanco El Pasaje
places.note: The city's oldest tabanco, wine from the cask and unamplified flamenco most nights.

places.name: Tabanco Plateros
places.note: Ideal spot for working through the sherry styles with small traditional tapas.

places.name: Bodegas Gonzalez Byass (Tio Pepe)
places.note: Historic bodega tour and tasting through the solera system where fino was born.

food.name: Brandy de Jerez
food.desc: Spirit aged in old sherry casks in the same solera system as the wine, giving a rounded, raisiny brandy found nowhere else in Spain.

places.name: Bodegas Fundador
places.note: Oldest bodega in Jerez and home of the original Spanish brandy; tastings daily.

places.name: Bodegas Lustau
places.note: Well-run visits covering both the sherries and the cask-aged brandies.

places.name: Tabanco Las Banderillas
places.note: Traditional bar where locals finish a night of tapas with a copa of brandy.

landmarks: Alcázar de Jerez
An 11th-century Moorish fortress of honey-colored stone, its octagonal tower, Arab baths and tranquil gardens overlook the city's tiled rooftops and sherry bodegas.
Catedral de Jerez (Cathedral of San Salvador)
A dramatic 17th-century blend of Gothic, baroque and neoclassical styles, its flying buttresses and freestanding bell tower rise theatrically above the harvest-festival steps.
Real Escuela Andaluza del Arte Ecuestre (Royal Andalusian School of Equestrian Art)
Home of the famed dancing Andalusian horses, this elegant 19th-century palace estate stages balletic dressage performances that define Jerez's equestrian soul.
Bodegas Tío Pepe (González Byass)
The world's most famous sherry house offers cellar tours past oak butts signed by celebrities, ending with tastings of crisp fino beneath vine-draped courtyards.
Cartuja de Santa María de la Defensión (Charterhouse)
A magnificent 15th-century Carthusian monastery outside town, its lavish baroque facade and serene cloisters make it Cádiz province's finest religious monument.
Iglesia de San Miguel
A flamboyant Gothic church begun in 1484, its intricately carved facade and soaring tower preside over the flamenco-steeped neighborhood where singer Lola Flores was born.
Plaza del Arenal
Jerez's grand central square, ringed by palm trees and cafés, has hosted everything from medieval jousts to today's feria crowds and motorcycle-race celebrations.
Tabanco El Pasaje
The city's oldest tabanco, pouring sherry straight from the barrel since 1925 while raw, spontaneous flamenco performances erupt just feet from your table.
Centro Andaluz de Documentación del Flamenco (Palacio Pemartín)
Housed in an 18th-century palace in the Santiago gypsy quarter, this archive and cultural center celebrates Jerez's claim as a cradle of flamenco art.
Bodegas Fundador
Founded in 1730, Jerez's oldest bodega complex ages brandy and sherry in cathedral-like cellars, including casks once destined for Magellan-era explorers' descendants.

train.note: No international trains. Frequent trains run to Cádiz in about 40 minutes and El Puerto de Santa María on the Cercanías C-1 line, to Seville in around an hour on Media Distancia services, and long-distance Alvia trains reach Madrid in about 4 hours. The station is east of the old town near the bus terminal. Booking opens around 60 days ahead.

bus.note: No international coaches. Comes and Damas run from the Jerez bus station beside the railway station to Cádiz, El Puerto, Sanlúcar, Ronda, Seville and the Costa de la Luz beaches; ALSA (https://www.alsa.com/en) covers the longer routes to Madrid. The train is quicker for Cádiz and Seville.

ferry.note: Jerez is inland with no port of its own. The nearest passenger sailings are the bay catamaran and the Canary Islands ferry from Cádiz, about 40 minutes away by train, and the Morocco crossings from Tarifa and Algeciras further south.

full.blurb: The Andalusian capital of flamenco, the Real Alcázar and a vast Gothic cathedral, about an hour north by train.
